title: inshallah or mashallah?
hookLine: two words people mix up: one looks ahead, one looks at what's already here
carry: inshallah for tomorrow, mashallah for today

cards: See you tomorrow? Inshallah. Will the report be done by Friday?
Inshallah. A cousin's new baby, a friend's new apartment, a kid's first goal: mashallah. They sound alike, they both have Allah in them, and people swap them around, Muslims included.
There's even a family joke that inshallah is the politest way to say probably not. The real difference fits in one line.

teach.b: In sha' Allah: if God wills. It looks ahead, at something that hasn't happened yet.
It comes from the eighteenth surah of the Qur'an, the Cave: “And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will.” So it isn't maybe. Maybe is about your mood.
Inshallah is about what you don't control. You plan completely, and admit that tomorrow isn't yours to hand out. It was never a reason to skip the work, either.
A man once asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ whether he should leave his camel untied and trust God. Tie it, came the answer, and trust. Now its twin.
Ma sha' Allah: what God has willed. It looks at something good that's already here: a baby, a new job, a view that stops you. It says, this is a gift, not only my doing.
And it comes from the same surah. A few verses on, a man walks proudly through his gardens, and his friend asks why he didn't say, on the way in, what God wills. So: inshallah for tomorrow.

how: Muslims add inshallah, "if God wills," when they speak of something they intend to do, following Qur'an 18:23–24, and say mashallah, "what God has willed," when they see or hear of something good: a new baby, good news, something beautiful.

games.q: which is which — tap the pairs.
p: what God has willed: already here
and trust: do your part first

s: that's the family joke. the word means if God wills: a real plan, with humility about tomorrow.
inshallah and mashallah both come from the same surah
surah 18: inshallah from verses 23–24, mashallah from the story of the gardens at verse 39.
mashallah is for plans you hope will happen
that's inshallah. mashallah is for good that's already here.

games.q: a man asks the Prophet ﷺ: should I leave my camel untied and trust God, or tie it up and trust God?
o: leave it loose. trust is enough.
tie it. trust is for things you can't do.
games.why: tie it, and trust. both, not one or the other: do your part completely, then hold the rest with an open hand.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, think of one thing you've planned for tomorrow. On the second, notice the part of it that's up to you, and the part that isn't.
On the third, think of one good thing already in your life, and let it be a gift.

wordCard.voice: Inshallah. If God wills: a real plan, held with an open hand. And its twin, mashallah, for what's already here. Fourth word.

orig.note: Arabic: "if God wills." in (if) + sha'a (wills) + Allah (God). its twin, ما شاء الله, ma sha' Allah, is "what God has willed."

carryVoice: Your line: inshallah for tomorrow, mashallah for today. That's the whole difference. That's day four.

sources.q: And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow, Except if Allah will.

sources.ref: Qur'an 18:32–44, esp. 18:39 (ma sha' Allah in the parable of the two gardens)
a well-known hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi (tie your camel and trust)
